newsitem.title: USA: US analysts say Argentina liquidity deal positive.
newsitem.headline: US analysts say Argentina liquidity deal positive.

text.p: Argentina's newly signed standby credit facility demonstrates confidence in the country's banking system and provides a viable line of defense against a run on Argentine banks, U.S. analysts said.

On Friday, Argentine officials said the country had received agreements from 13 international banks to repurchase up to $6.1 billion of Argentine government securities in the event of a banking crisis.
Analysts said the deal provides both protection for Argentine banks and comfort for investors.
"This is very positive for Argentina," said Joyce Chang, emerging markets debt strategist at Merrill Lynch. "It gives them a cushion if they ever were to have to draw on it."
Although Argentina may never need to borrow under the agreement, its ability to raise credit from foreign banks "shows there is a lot of confidence in Argentina," Chang said.
Pedro Pou, president of Argentina's central bank, told reporters earlier today that the credit facility almost certainly will be unutilized.
"It's like an insurance policy," he said. "We don't anticipate having the accident."

In March 1995, soon after the Mexican peso devaluation, Argentina suffered a run on liquidity, which Pou said drained about $15 billion from the country's gross domestic product. He said the new credit agreement, which costs about $18 million a year to maintain, is a cheap vaccination against another such crisis.
"It's not only an insurance policy, it's also a comfort for those planning investments in Argentina," said David Malpass, chief international economist at Bear Stearns & Co.
Malpass said investors would feel more secure knowing that Argentina has instant access to foreign credit, even if there were no fear of a domestic crisis.
"The timing is coming from strength," Malpass said. "It's excellent timing, because (Argentina is) riding pretty high -- they've had a pretty successful second half of 1996."
Malpass said the credit agreement offers "a material addition to their existing availability."

Argentina will pay about $18 million a year for at least the next two years to keep the credit facility waiting in the wings. It would pay interest of about 2.07 percent more than the London Interbank Offered Rate on any borrowings under the facility.
